title: The Gut Microbiome and Cancer Therapy
body_text: Here’s some work that ties in with that post I did the other day about bacterial associations with cancer (or the general lack of same). It’s been known for some time that cancer immunotherapy responses are influenced by the human microbiome - for example, antibiotic treatment seems to really dampen the effects of PD-L1-directed antibodies, which is of course not what you want to see. One hypothesis for this had to do with the idea of particular bacteria being associated with particular forms of cancer, but that looks less likely now that we see that most tumors outside of the GI tract aren’t associated with bacteria much at all. So what does that leave you with? This new paper finds an unexpected pathway: bile acids. When you take oral antibiotics, your gut microflora are of course disrupted. There’s no way around that. And those bacteria are of course sitting around down there using whatever they can find for food - things our digestive system can’t break down itself, digestion products themselves, whatever. And the bile acids that are added in from the liver (via the gall bladder) are definitely part of that setup. The authors here find the “dysbiosis” caused by antibiotic treatment tends to produce a larger proportion of bile acids that have been conjugated to taurine by the remaining bacteria (who now have more of a scope for their activities). The Enterocloster genus seems to be particularly involved. And as it happens, bile acids of this type had already been seen to affect T-cell function and other immune responses in liver cancer and indeed to regulate a number of T-cell responses. The taurine-conjugated species seem to make activated T cells less viable overall, and they also hit the FXR nuclear receptor, with downstream effects that include T-cell exhaustion. Treating animals with excess Entercloster bacteria could recapitulate these problems, as did bile duct ligation. Also in animal models, these effects can be countered by administering an FXR agonist, or doing a fecal microbial transplantThe authors go on to show that increased amounts of these tauro-bile acids in the plasma are associated with lower survival after immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment, and that checking for elevated gamma-glutamyl transferase as a sign of trouble with the liver-gut axis might be enough of an outcomes market by itself. This means that avoiding antibiotic therapy when possible would be a good idea in cancer patients treated with checkpoint inhibitors, and it also means that these patients - and in fact, probably other cancer patients as well - could benefit from attempts to strengthen the bile acid and bile acid metabolite production. All these things (the liver, the bile, the small intestine, the microbiome, and the T-cell immune response) are connected, and people should really be aware of this. At the very least, we might be able to tell which patients are most likely to benefit from immunotherapy and work from there.
